(Surat al-'Asr)
Three verses, Makkan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By time (al-'asr)﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By time (al-'asr)﴾ Know that they have mentioned several opinions in the interpretation of al-'asr:

The first: that it is time (ad-dahr). The one who holds this advances several arguments:

The first: what is reported "from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he swore by time (ad-dahr)", and "he (peace be upon him) used to recite: 'By al-'asr and the vicissitudes of time (nawa'ib ad-dahr)'." But we say: this would invalidate the prayer, so we do not say that he recited it as Qur'an, but rather as explanation. Perhaps the Exalted did not mention ad-dahr because He knew that the heretic is fond of mentioning and glorifying it; for that reason He mentioned it in ﴿Has there not come﴾ [al-Insan: 1], as a refutation of the corruption of their claim of nature and time (at-tab' wa-ad-dahr).

The second: that time comprises wonders, for in it come joy and hardship, health and sickness, wealth and poverty. Rather, in it is what is more wondrous than every wonder: the intellect cannot judge it to be non-existent, for it is divided and partitioned into year, month, day and hour, and is judged to increase, decrease and correspond, and to be past and future; so how could it be non-existent? Yet the intellect cannot judge it to exist either, because the present cannot be divided, and the past and the future are non-existent; so how can existence be ascribed to it?

The third: that the remainder of a person's life has no price. If you wasted a thousand years and then repented in the last moment of life, you would remain in Paradise forever and ever. Then you would know that the noblest of things is your life in that moment. So it is as though time and age are among the roots of blessings, and for that reason He swore by it and alerted us that night and day are an opportunity that the accountable person squanders. To this points His saying: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeeding each other, for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to show gratitude﴾ [al-Furqan: 62].

The fourth: that His saying in Surat al-An'am: ﴿Say: To whom belongs what is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God﴾ [al-An'am: 12] is a pointer to place and what is in place; then He said: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day﴾ [al-An'am: 13], which is a pointer to time and what is in time. We have explained there that time

is higher and nobler than place. Since that is so, the oath by al-'asr is an oath by the nobler of the two halves of God's dominion and sovereignty.

The fifth: that they used to attribute loss to the vicissitudes of time. So it is as though the Exalted swore that time and the age are a blessing present and without fault; the one at loss and at fault is only the human being.

The sixth: that He mentioned the age (al-'asr) whose passing diminishes your life. If nothing is earned in return, that diminishing becomes the very loss itself, and for that reason He said: ﴿is in loss﴾. Among this is the saying of the poet:

"We rejoice in the days we complete, yet every day that passes is a reduction of the appointed term."

So the meaning is as though: By the age whose affair is wondrous, in that the human being rejoices at its passing, thinking he has found profit, though it is the demolition of his life; and he is truly in loss.

The second opinion: that of Abu Muslim: what is meant by al-'asr is one of the two ends of the day. The reasons for this are several:

The first: that the Exalted swore by al-'asr as He swore by the forenoon (ad-duha), because both contain proofs of His power. Every morning is like the Resurrection: people come out of the graves, the dead become alive, and the scales are set up; and every evening resembles the ruin of the world through the thunderbolt and death. Each of these two states is a just witness. Then, if a judge does not rule after two witnesses, he is counted a loser; so likewise the human being heedless of them is in loss.

The second: al-Hasan (may God have mercy on him) said: He swore by this time only as a warning that the markets are near their closing and the end of trade and earning in them. If you have not earned, and you enter the house and your family gathers around you, each asking you for what is his due, then you will be ashamed and be among the losers. So likewise we say: By al-'asr, that is, the age of the world: the Resurrection has drawn near, and you have not yet prepared, nor known that tomorrow you will be asked about the bounty in which you lived in your worldly life, and asked about your dealings with creation, and each one of the wronged will claim what is owed by you. Then you are a loser. Its parallel is: ﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near to them, while they are in heedlessness, turning away﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1].

The third: that this time is held in esteem, and the proof is his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever swears falsely after 'asr, God will not speak to him nor look at him on the Day of Resurrection." So as He swore by the forenoon concerning the one who profits, likewise He swore by al-'asr concerning the one who loses. For He swore by the forenoon concerning the one who profits and gave the Messenger glad tidings that his matter was heading to ascendancy, and here, concerning the one who loses, He warned him that his matter is heading to decline. Then it is as though He says: part of the day remains, so He urges him to make up for it in the remainder through repentance. It is related from one of the Salaf: "I learned the meaning of the surah from a seller of ice, who would cry out and say: 'Have mercy on one whose capital is melting! Have mercy on one whose capital is melting!' So I said: this is the meaning of ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾: the afternoon passes over him, his life goes by, and he earns nothing, so he is a loser."

The third opinion: that of Muqatil: he meant the 'Asr prayer. They mention several arguments for it:

The first: that the Exalted swore by the 'Asr prayer because of its merit, by the proof of His saying ﴿and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], which in the codex of Hafsah is "the 'Asr prayer"; and it was said regarding His saying: ﴿you detain them after the prayer, and they swear by God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106] that it is the 'Asr prayer.

The second: his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever misses the 'Asr prayer, it is as if he has been robbed of his family and his property."

The third: that the obligation in performing it is harder, because of people's rush in their trades and earnings at the end of the day and their preoccupation with their livelihoods.

The fourth: it is reported "that a woman was crying out in the lanes of Madinah and saying: 'Show me the Prophet (ﷺ)!' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw her and asked her what had happened. She said: 'O Messenger of God, my husband was away from me and I committed adultery, and a child came to me from adultery, so I threw the child into a jar of vinegar until he died, and then we sold that vinegar. Is there repentance for me?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'As for adultery, the stoning penalty is upon you; as for killing the child, its recompense is Hell; and as for selling the vinegar, you have committed

Page 82
a grave sin; but I thought that you had abandoned the 'Asr prayer.'" So in this hadith is a pointer to the magnification of the matter of this prayer.

The fifth: that by the 'Asr prayer the day's acts of obedience are sealed. So it is like repentance, by which deeds are sealed. Just as bequeathing repentance is obligatory, so is it with the 'Asr prayer, since matters are judged by their endings. So He swore by this prayer to magnify its standing, to add emphasis to the accountable person's charge to perform it, and as a pointer from Him that if you perform it properly, your loss turns into profit, as He said: ﴿except those who believe﴾.

The sixth: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There are three whom God will not look at on the Day of Resurrection, nor speak to them, nor purify them", and among them he counted "a man who swore falsely after 'Asr."

(If it is said:) The 'Asr prayer is our act, so how can it be said that God the Exalted swore by it?

The answer: it is not an oath insofar as it is our act, but insofar as it is a noble matter by which God the Exalted has made us worship.

The fourth opinion: that it is an oath by the time of the Messenger (peace be upon him). They argue for it with his saying (peace be upon him): "Your likeness and the likeness of those before you is that of a man who hired laborers and said: 'Who will work from dawn to noon for a qirat?' So the Jews worked. Then he said: 'Who will work from noon to 'asr for a qirat?' So the Christians worked. Then he said: 'Who will work from 'asr to sunset for two qirats?' And you worked. The Jews and the Christians grew angry and said: 'We did more work and received less pay!' God said: 'Have I diminished anything of your wages?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'Then that is My bounty, which I give to whom I will.'" So this report indicates that al-'asr is the time particular to him and to his community, so inevitably God swore by it. So His saying ﴿By al-'asr﴾ means: by the age in which you are. He, the Exalted, swore by his time in this verse, by his place in His saying ﴿and you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], and by his life in His saying ﴿By your life﴾ [al-Hijr: 72]. So it is as though He said: by your age, your city and your life, all of which are like a container for him. If glorifying the container is obligatory, then judge the state of what is contained. Then He directed the oath, as though the Exalted were saying: You, Muhammad, were present among them and called them, and they turned away from you and paid you no heed; so how great is their loss and how grave their abandonment.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾. There are several issues here:

**First issue:** The alif and lam in "al-insan" (mankind) may signify the genus, or it may refer to a specific, previously known referent. For this reason the commentators mention two views on it:

The first: that what is meant is the genus, as in the saying, "Dirhams have become plentiful in the hands of the people." What indicates this view is the exception of those who believe from among mankind.

The second view: that what is meant is a specific individual. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means a group of the polytheists, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Abu Lahab. In a report traced back to the Prophet (marfu'), it is Abu Jahl. It is also narrated that these men used to say, "Muhammad is in loss," so the Exalted swore that the matter is the opposite of what they imagine.

**Second issue:** "Khusr" is "khusran" (loss), just as "kufr" is said for "kufran." Its meaning is diminution and the loss of one's capital. Then

[Page 83]
there are two interpretations of it. If we take "mankind" to mean the genus, then the meaning of loss is the ruin of one's self and one's lifespan, except for the believer who does righteous deeds, for his lifespan and wealth are not ruined, because through them he has earned everlasting happiness. If we take the word "mankind" to mean the disbeliever, then what is meant is that he is in misguidance and disbelief, except for whoever among them believes, for then he is delivered from that loss into profit.

**Third issue:** He said ﴿in loss﴾ (lafi khusrin) and did not say "in the loss" (lafi al-khusri), because indefiniteness (tankir) sometimes conveys magnification and at other times belittlement. If we take it in the first sense, the meaning is: mankind is in a great loss whose true extent none knows but God. The explanation is that a sin grows great according to the greatness of the one against whom it is committed, or because it occurs in return for great blessings; both aspects are present in the servant's sin against his Lord, so inevitably that sin is of the utmost gravity. If we take it in the second sense, the meaning is that the loss of man is less than the loss of Satan, and in this is a glad tiding: that among My creation there is one more disobedient than you. The sound interpretation is the first.

**Fourth issue:** Someone might say: His words ﴿in loss﴾ convey singularity, although man is in various kinds of loss.

The answer: the true loss is his being deprived of serving his Lord. As for the rest, namely being deprived of Paradise and falling into the Fire, in relation to the first they are as nothing. This is like the fact that there are many benefits in man's existence, and yet He said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. That is, since this purpose is the most exalted of purposes, all other purposes in relation to it are as nothing.

Know that God, the Exalted, joined to this verse indications showing His emphasis in explaining that man is in loss:

The first: His words ﴿in loss﴾ convey that he is as if immersed in loss, and that it surrounds him from every side.

The second: the word "inna" (indeed), for it is for emphasis.

The third: the particle lam in "lafi khusr."

Here there are two possibilities:

The first: that ﴿in loss﴾ means "on the path of loss," as in His words about consuming the property of orphans: ﴿They only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], since its outcome is the Fire.

The second possibility: that man is never free of loss, because loss is the squandering of capital, and a man's capital is his lifespan, and he is rarely free of squandering his lifespan. For every hour that passes over a person: if it is spent in disobedience, there is no doubt of loss; if it is occupied with permissible things, loss is still present, for once it has gone no trace of it remains, although he was able to do in it a deed whose effect would remain forever; and if it is occupied with acts of obedience, there is no act of obedience except that it is possible to perform it, or something else, in a better way, because the degrees of humility and submission to God are unlimited, since the degrees of God's majesty and might are unlimited, and the more a person knows of them, the greater his fear of Him, the Exalted, and so his veneration when performing acts of obedience is more complete and perfect. Leaving the higher and settling for the lower is a kind of loss. Thus it is established that man is never at all free from some kind of loss.

Know that this verse is like a warning that the basic state of man is to be in loss and disappointment. The explanation is that man's happiness lies in loving the Hereafter and turning away from the world, yet the causes that call to the Hereafter are hidden, while the causes that call to love of the world are manifest, namely the five senses, desire and anger. For this reason most of creation became occupied with love of the world, immersed in seeking it, and so they were in loss and perdition. If it is said: He, the Exalted, said in Surat

[Page 84]
al-Tin: ﴿We certainly created man in the best of forms﴾ ﴿then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 4-5], so there it indicates that the beginning is from perfection and the end is in deficiency, whereas here it indicates that the beginning is from deficiency and the end is in perfection; how then can the two be reconciled?

We say: What is mentioned in Surat al-Tin concerns the states of the body, while here it concerns the states of the soul, so there is no contradiction between the two statements.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾.

Know that faith (iman) and righteous deeds have already been explained several times. Here, then, are several issues:

**Issue One:** Those who hold that deeds are not included in the meaning of "faith" argue that God, the Exalted, joined "doing righteous deeds" to faith by conjunction. Had righteous deeds been included in the meaning of faith, this would be a repetition. Nor can it be said that such repetition occurs in the Qur'an, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7], and His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. For we say that in those cases the repetition is fitting because restating the item indicates that it is the noblest kind within that general class, whereas righteous deeds are not the noblest of the things called faith. So this interpretation is invalid.

Al-Halimi said: This repetition certainly occurs, because even if faith does not include righteous deeds, His saying ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ does include faith, so His saying ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ would make the mention of "those who believe" unnecessary. Moreover, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ includes ﴿and enjoin one another to the truth, and enjoin one another to patience﴾, so that too would necessarily be repetition.

The first group answered: We do not deny that repetition may occur for the sake of emphasis, but the default is that it does not, and this much suffices for the argument.

**Issue Two:** Those who decisively affirm the threat of punishment for the sinners (fussaq) argue from this verse. They said: The verse indicates that man is in loss absolutely, and then makes an exception: ﴿those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. What is made conditional on two conditions is absent when either one is absent. So we know that whoever lacks faith and righteous deeds must be in loss, in this world and the next. Since those who combine these two qualities are extremely few, and loss is inevitable for whoever does not combine them, those who are saved are fewer than those who perish. Even if the saved were the majority, the fear would be great, lest you not be among the few; how then when the saved are the fewer? Should the fear not be all the more intense!

**Issue Three:** This exception contains three points:

First: it is a consolation for the believer over the loss of his life and youth, because deeds have brought him to something better than his life and youth.

Second: it is a reminder that whatever calls you to obey God is righteousness (salah), and whatever distracts you from God toward something else is corruption (fasad).

Third: the Mu'tazilah said: Calling the deeds "righteous deeds" is a reminder that the reason for their goodness is not what the Ash'ariyyah claim, but that the command came only because they in themselves contain aspects of righteousness. The Ash'ariyyah replied that God, the Exalted, described them as righteous without clarifying whether they are righteous because of aspects inherent in them or because of the command.

**Issue Four:** A questioner may ask: On the side of loss He mentioned the ruling and did not mention the cause, while on the side of gain He mentioned the cause, namely faith and righteous deeds, and did not mention the ruling. What is the difference?

We say: He did not mention the cause of loss because loss comes about through action, which is committing disobedience, and also through omission, which is not undertaking obedience. Gain, however, comes about only through action. So He mentioned the cause of gain, which is deeds. There is another aspect: on the side of loss He was general and gave no detail, while on the side of gain He gave detail and explanation, and this befits generosity.

*As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and enjoin one another to the truth, and enjoin one another to patience﴾.*

Know that when God, the Exalted, made clear regarding those excepted that through their faith and righteous deeds they have gone out of being in loss and become people of felicity, since they held fast to what leads them to attain reward and be saved from punishment, He then described them as having become, because of their intense love of obedience, unwilling to limit themselves to what concerns them alone. Rather they urge others to follow their path, so as to be a cause of others' obedience too, as people of religion should be. In this sense the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. Mutual enjoining of the truth includes the rest of the religion, in knowledge and action, and mutual enjoining of patience includes driving the soul to bear the hardship of obligation, in performing what is required and avoiding what is forbidden; for undertaking what is disliked and holding back from what is desired are both severely hard. Here are several issues:

**Issue One:** This verse contains a severe threat, because God, the Exalted, judged all people to be in loss except those who bring these four things: faith, righteous deeds, mutual enjoining of the truth, and mutual enjoining of patience. This shows that salvation depends on all of these together, and that just as the person under obligation must secure what concerns himself, so toward others too he has duties, among them calling to the religion, giving sincere advice, enjoining the right and forbidding the wrong, and loving for him what he loves for himself. Then He repeated the mutual enjoining so that the first would include calling to God and the second steadfastness upon it; or the first enjoining the right and the second forbidding the wrong. From this is His saying: ﴿and forbid what is wrong, and be patient﴾ [Luqman: 17]. 'Umar said: May God have mercy on the one who gifts me my faults.

**Issue Two:** The verse shows that the truth is heavy and that trials accompany it; for that reason He paired it with mutual enjoining.

**Issue Three:** He said "وتَواصَوْا" (they enjoined one another, past tense) and not "ويَتَواصَوْنَ" (they enjoin one another, present tense), so that it would not be taken as a command; rather the aim is to praise them for what has proceeded from them in the past, and that inspires in them the desire to remain steadfast in it in the future.

**Issue Four:** Abu 'Amr recited "بِالصَّبْرِ" with an ishmam (a slight hint) of the ba', not fully pronounced. Abu 'Ali said: This is permissible in pausing, and it does not occur in continuous reading except by treating connection like pausing, which hardly ever occurs in recitation. In the same way is what is reported from Sallam ibn al-Mundhir, that he recited "والعَصِرْ" with a kasrah on the sad; perhaps he paused because his breath ran out or because of some incident that prevented him from continuing the recitation. It should be understood in this way, not as treating connection like pausing. And God, glory be to Him, the Exalted, knows best. May God bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
